title: Replication and Read-After-Write Consistency
summary: A successful save can still look old on a replica. Plan read freshness, failover and recovery separately so users know what to expect.
body:
Replication copies data to another server, but 'we have replicas' does not specify when a write is safe or what a read can see. Start with the write acknowledgement and the read path. Interviewers probe this whenever a design adds read replicas to scale reads, promises high availability for a database, or has a user who edits something and immediately looks at it.

## Trace a write and a read

A primary records a profile update and acknowledges it. With asynchronous replication, another server may not have received or replayed that update yet. If the next read goes to that replica, the user can see the old profile even though the update succeeded. This is a read-after-write problem, not necessarily a failed write.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    APP["App servers"] -->|"writes"| P[("Primary")]
    P -->|"WAL stream, sync ack"| S1[("Sync standby")]
    P -->|"WAL stream, async"| R1[("Read replica 1")]
    P -->|"WAL stream, async"| R2[("Read replica 2")]
    APP -->|"lag-tolerant reads"| R1
    APP -->|"lag-tolerant reads"| R2
    APP -->|"fresh reads"| P
```

Every write goes to the primary, which streams its write-ahead log (WAL) to three copies. The synchronous standby must confirm before the primary acknowledges a commit, so it is the safe failover target. The two asynchronous read replicas apply the log when they can, typically milliseconds behind but seconds or minutes during load spikes, long transactions or network trouble. The application routes lag-tolerant reads to them and freshness-sensitive reads to the primary. Note that the read replicas add read capacity but not write capacity: each one replays every write.

## Compare acknowledgement policies

| Policy | Benefit | Cost or limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asynchronous replication | The primary need not wait for a remote acknowledgement | Replicas may lag; promoting a lagging replica can lose acknowledged writes |
| Synchronous replication | A configured replica acknowledgement participates in committing the write | Network and replica delays affect write latency and availability |
| Quorum synchronous (any one of several standbys) | Bounded data loss with tolerance for one slow standby | Still adds a round trip; needs at least two standbys to avoid stalls |
| Read from primary after a write | A straightforward way to obtain a fresh read from the same authoritative primary | Adds primary load and still requires a defined failover policy |

'Synchronous' alone is not a complete guarantee. Ask whether the remote node has received, durably stored or applied the record. PostgreSQL exposes this as distinct `synchronous_commit` levels (`remote_write`, `on`, `remote_apply`), so avoid claiming every synchronous replica can immediately serve the new value. A synchronous standby in another region adds that region's round trip, often 30 to 80 ms, to every commit; that cost is why many systems replicate synchronously within a region and asynchronously across regions.

## Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless

Most designs use **single-leader** replication: one primary accepts writes, which gives a single order of writes and simple reasoning. **Multi-leader** replication accepts writes in several places (for example, one leader per region) to cut write latency, at the price of concurrent conflicting writes that need a resolution rule. **Leaderless** stores such as Cassandra write to several replicas directly and use read and write quorums, which tolerate node failures without failover but offer weaker ordering. In an interview, default to single-leader and justify anything else with a concrete need such as multi-region writes.

## Choose freshness per operation

A public view count may tolerate lag. Showing a just-saved address or deciding whether a user is authorized usually needs stronger handling. Options include routing sensitive reads to the primary, using a version or log-position token and waiting for a replica to catch up, or explicitly returning a pending state. A fixed delay after writing is a heuristic, not a correctness guarantee: lag changes under load.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant API as API
    participant P as Primary
    participant R as Replica
    U->>API: save new address
    API->>P: UPDATE, COMMIT
    P-->>API: committed at log position 1042
    API-->>U: ok, token 1042
    U->>API: GET address, token 1042
    API->>R: replayed position?
    R-->>API: 1039
    alt replica behind token
        API->>P: read from primary
    else replica caught up
        API->>R: read from replica
    end
    API-->>U: new address
```

The write returns the commit's log position (in PostgreSQL, an LSN; in MySQL, a GTID), and the client sends it back on the next read, in a cookie or header. The API checks how far the chosen replica has replayed. Here the replica is at 1039, behind the token, so the read goes to the primary (or waits briefly for the replica). Once the replica passes 1042 it can serve the read. This gives read-your-writes for that user without sending everyone's reads to the primary. A simpler variant pins a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, but that is still a heuristic sized to typical lag. Related guarantees: **monotonic reads** (a user never sees time go backward, achieved by pinning a session to one replica or by tracking the highest position seen) and **consistent prefix reads** (a reply never appears before the message it answers).

## Failover is a protocol

A health check can suspect a failed primary but cannot prove it has stopped writing. Promotion requires coordination and fencing so the old primary cannot keep accepting authoritative writes. Define how clients discover the new primary and how connection pools recover. State the expected recovery time and which acknowledged writes might be missing. Typical automated failover, such as Patroni with etcd or a managed database service, completes in tens of seconds to a couple of minutes, during which writes fail and should be retried idempotently.

Read replicas mainly spread reads. They do not automatically scale writes, eliminate hot keys or replace backups. Accidental deletion can replicate perfectly to every copy. Recovery from deletion needs an independent recovery mechanism, such as base backups plus archived WAL for point-in-time recovery, and a tested restore process.

## Failure modes and common mistakes

- Treating replica lag as a constant. Monitor it (`pg_stat_replication`, `replay_lag`) and alert on it; a long-running query on a replica can delay replay or be cancelled.
- Promoting the most convenient replica instead of the most up-to-date one.
- Failing over without fencing, producing two primaries that both accept writes.
- Adding replicas to fix a write bottleneck.
- Counting replicas as backups.

## How to use it in an interview

Say which operations read from where: "Feed and profile views read from replicas and may be a second stale; a user's own just-edited profile and all authorization checks read from the primary or use a log-position token." Give the numbers that justify it: read-to-write ratio (replicas help when reads dominate, say 20 to 1), typical and worst-case lag, and the recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) implied by your acknowledgement policy. Expect follow-ups: "the primary dies, what is lost?", "how do clients find the new primary?", and "a replica falls 10 minutes behind, what do users see?".

## Interview exercise

A user changes a shipping address, then immediately places an order. Which read must see the new address? Draw a read policy for this flow, then explain what happens during primary failover. Contrast it with a product-page view count where a short freshness delay is acceptable.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL: standby servers and streaming replication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html) documents replication lag, acknowledgement choices and standby promotion.
- [PostgreSQL: synchronous_commit and WAL settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html) defines what each synchronous level waits for.
keyTakeaways: Define acknowledgement and replay semantics rather than treating all replicas as equally fresh.
Asynchronous failover can lose acknowledged writes that have not reached the promoted replica.
Route or coordinate freshness-sensitive reads explicitly; a fixed sleep is not a guarantee.
Replication is not a backup or a complete failover protocol.
